templates.stem: If $(a - {=h}, b + {=k}) = ({=u}, {=v})$, find $a$ and $b$, then plot the point $(a, b)$.
solution: Equal ordered pairs have equal first components and equal second components.
Plot $({=tx}, {=ty})$: go along the x-axis first, then up or down.
templates.notes: Targets kept within the -5..5 grid (the book's x=7,y=2 would be off-grid). wrong-quadrant and off-target are arithmetic/sign slips, not the order misconception, so left unmapped.

templates.stem: If $X=\{2, -1\}$ and $Y=\{4, 0\}$, build $X\times Y$ by selecting all its ordered pairs.
solution: In $X\times Y$ the first component comes from $X$ and the second from $Y$.
templates.notes: missing-pairs could reflect adding set sizes (adds-set-sizes) but more likely just an incomplete listing; not mapped to avoid a weak diagnosis.

templates.stem: If $Y=\{4, 0\}$ and $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$, build $Y\times Z$ by selecting all its ordered pairs.
solution: First components come from $Y$, second components from $Z$.
templates.notes: Spec X/Y fields hold Y and Z of the book question.

gaps.description: Two columns of dots (set X on the left, Y on the right); the student draws arrows to construct the arrow diagram of X×Y (or X×X), with the matching list of ordered pairs updating live. It would diagnose missing arrows (incomplete product), arrows drawn in the wrong direction (reversed order, Y×X), and arrows only between equal elements (treating X×X as the identity pairs).
gaps.why: No existing kind draws arrows between two sets; product_builder only selects pairs from a list and does not teach the arrow diagram or the cartesian diagram representation.

gaps.description: On a coordinate net the student shades the region representing a product of intervals such as $[-2,3]\times[-2,3]$ (or N×N, Z×Z dots) and then taps points to test membership. It would diagnose shading only the axes or boundary, using the wrong interval for one coordinate, and treating a continuous product as a finite set of dots.
gaps.why: pair_plotter only places a single lattice point, and the objective's misconception list is empty, so no honest diagnostic mapping exists for point plotting; the interval-product region needs a shading instrument.

records.notes: Two templates cover LO1 (pair_plotter) and LO2 (product_builder). LO3 and LO4 are recorded as gaps.

gaps.description: The student sees X, Y and a rule such as b = 2a + 4 or 'a is a digit of b'. She taps, from the full grid of X×Y, exactly the ordered pairs that satisfy the rule. Anchor example: X={-1,1,2}, Y={2,4,6,8}, expected {(-1,2),(1,6),(2,8)}. Errors it would report: a pair missing, a pair that fails the rule, a pair written (b, a), a pair outside X×Y, and a pair found by a sign slip such as 2a−4.
gaps.why: product_builder grades against the whole of X×Y, so it cannot ask for a rule-defined subset. pair_plotter takes one lattice point, not a set, and would only check one value of the rule. Both would be answer boxes in disguise. In addition, this objective lists no misconceptions, so a diagnostics mapping is impossible under FR-1215.

gaps.need_kind: relation_diagram (arrow diagram and cartesian diagram drawer)
gaps.description: The student is given a relation as a set of pairs, or by its rule. She draws arrows from elements of X to elements of Y in two side-by-side ovals, and the same pairs appear live as points on a cartesian grid (or the reverse). Anchor example: the additive-inverse relation on {-2,-1,0,1,2}, giving arrows -2→2, -1→1, 0→0, 1→-1, 2→-2. Errors it would report: arrows reversed in direction, a missing arrow (for example the loop 0→0), an extra arrow, and cartesian points with x and y swapped.
gaps.why: No existing kind draws arrows between two sets. pair_plotter marks only one point and does not link the diagram to the arrow form. Representing the same relation in both forms is the whole objective. Also, no misconceptions are registered for this objective.

gaps.need_kind: relation_subset_sorter (is it a subset of X×Y?)
gaps.description: Given X, Y and a candidate set of pairs, the student sorts each pair as 'in X×Y' or 'not in X×Y', and then states whether the set is a relation from X to Y. For a relation on X she checks that R ⊂ X×X. She would also pick which pairs satisfy the stated rule. Errors it would report: a pair accepted although one entry is not in X or Y, a valid pair rejected, and the reversed order (b, a) accepted for X to Y.
gaps.why: product_builder builds the entire product X×Y. It cannot model a subset chosen by a rule or the yes/no test of membership. Using it would be a forced fit. The objective has no anchor question and no misconceptions in the lesson file, so any template would also have no valid misconception ids.

records.notes: I wrote no templates. First, all three objectives have empty misconception lists, so no diagnostics mapping is legal under FR-1215, and the schema requires at least one. Second, no existing kind genuinely fits. product_builder builds the whole X×Y rather than a rule-defined subset, and pair_plotter handles a single point. Using either would be a forced fit. Lesson 2 needs one or more new kinds, listed in the gaps. Samuel should also add misconceptions to these objectives, such as reversed pairs, missing the 0→0 pair, and sign slips in b = 2a + 4.

gaps.description: Two columns of dots (X on the left, Y on the right). The student drags arrows from elements of X to elements of Y. Two modes. (1) Build: draw a relation such as 'a = ½b' as arrows, or a relation that IS a function. (2) Repair: given a relation, add or remove arrows so that it becomes a function. The grading property is that every element of X has exactly one outgoing arrow, which the widget can light up live. It could also ask the student to construct a relation that is NOT a function, so they discover what fails. Predicates it could report: an element of X with two images, an element of X with no image, an arrow ending outside Y, and an arrow drawn in the wrong direction (Y to X).
gaps.why: Identifying a function means checking that each x has exactly one image. product_builder selects all pairs of X×Y, which is a different task. pair_plotter places one point and cannot express the one-image rule. An answer box would only test the verdict 'function / not function', not the construction. The objective also has no misconceptions listed, so any template would need ids added first.

gaps.description: The student sees a function given as a set of ordered pairs. They build the matching arrow diagram and the matching cartesian diagram by placing arrows and grid points, and the widget shows the three views changing together. A second mode gives f(x) = ax + b and a domain, and the student places the points. The widget would check that the diagram and the pair set agree. Predicates it could report: pairs read as (y, x), a missing pair, and an extra pair.
gaps.why: The objective is about moving between the symbolic form, the arrow diagram and the cartesian diagram. pair_plotter plots only one point and has no arrow-diagram view. There is no link between several representations of one set of pairs. No misconceptions are listed for this objective.

gaps.description: The student is given a function as arrows between X and Y and taps the elements that make up the domain, the codomain and the range. Elements of Y with no incoming arrow, such as 2 in the book example, stay in the codomain but drop out of the range. The student marks the range and sees it sit inside the codomain as a subset. Predicates it could report: range given as the whole codomain, range given as the domain, and an element of the range left out.
gaps.why: The core idea is that the range is the subset of the codomain that is actually reached. number_line_marker could tap a set of numbers, but it is a stretch. Sets like {2, 3, 5, 7} are not naturally laid out on a line, the range limit stops at 6, and it has no notion of codomain or of arrows. That would be an answer box in disguise. No misconceptions are listed for this objective.

templates.stem: Draw the graph of the linear function $f(x) = {=linear(m, b)}$. Drag two points so that the line is its graph.
solution: Write the rule as $y = f(x)$ and find two ordered pairs.
Put $x = 0$: $y = b$, so the graph cuts the y-axis at $(0, b)$. This point is not the origin when the rule has a constant term.
Put $x = 1$: $y = m + b$, a second ordered pair.
Plot the two pairs and draw the straight line through them.
templates.notes: The anchor list for lo:pp3u1-4-3 is empty, so parent_question_id is left blank. Samuel should assign the book's graphing exercise. Only intercept-wrong is mapped: the correct slope with the line forced through (0, 0) is the signature of the origin misconception. A student who has the right slope but the wrong intercept for another reason would also fire it. slope-sign-flipped, slope-inverted, vertical-line and off-target are left unmapped because this objective has no misconception that names them. The instances are all inside the instrument limits: whole-number m, |m| ≤ 5, b in −5..5. A constant-function instance (m = 0) could be added as a later row.

gaps.description: The student is given a function rule such as $x(x-2x^2)$, $x^2-(x^2-3)$ or $x^3+\frac{1}{x}+7$. They expand and simplify it by dropping term tiles into place. They then tag each term's power of x as a whole number or not, and read off the degree of the simplified polynomial. Errors it could diagnose: degree read before simplifying (the power in the brackets is taken), and 1/x or √x terms accepted as polynomial terms.
gaps.why: None of the existing kinds builds or classifies algebraic expressions. An answer box would be an answer box in disguise, so this is a gap and not a forced fit.

gaps.description: The student drags the vertex and one more point to build the graph of a quadratic such as $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$. They mark the vertex and the axis of symmetry and say whether the turning point is a maximum or a minimum. Errors it could diagnose: the vertex x-coordinate sign flipped, the axis drawn through the y-axis, a maximum and minimum mixed up, and the parabola opening the wrong way.
gaps.why: line_drawer cannot draw curves. The curve_sketcher kind is named in the contract, but its predicates and limits were not given for this lesson. If it is confirmed to cover quadratics with vertex and axis grading, it would fit. This objective also has no listed misconceptions or anchor questions.

gaps.description: The student substitutes a value, including a surd such as √3, into f(x) and builds the simplified image step by step. For example, $f(\sqrt{3}) = 3 - \sqrt{3} + 3 = 6-\sqrt{3}$. Errors it could diagnose: $(\sqrt{3})^2$ left unsimplified, and sign errors when substituting a negative value.
gaps.why: This is symbolic arithmetic with no spatial or constructive instrument among the existing kinds, so any widget would just be an answer box. The objective also has no listed misconceptions.

records.notes: I wrote one template, a line_drawer for lo:pp3u1-4-3. It fits because the misconception is that every line goes through the origin, and the student can see the intercept they place. The other three objectives are recorded as gaps. The anchor list for 4-3 is empty, so the template's parent_question_id is blank and needs assigning.
